questions.question: What property must a solid material have for liquid particles to be able to diffuse through it?
options: The material must be completely impermeable.
The material must be permeable to the liquid.
The material must contain active transport pumps.
The material must be metallic.

questions.question: When observing a colored liquid diffusing into a clear jelly cube, what pattern of color change is seen?
options: The color spreads from the outside edges inwards towards the center.
The center of the cube turns colored first, leaving the edges clear.
The entire cube changes color instantaneously all at once.
The color only stays on the bottom surface of the cube.

questions.question: If you increase the temperature of the liquid surrounding a jelly cube, what effect will this have on the rate of diffusion?
options: It will slow down diffusion because particles lose kinetic energy.
It will have no effect on diffusion.
It will speed up diffusion because the liquid particles move faster with more kinetic energy.
It will stop diffusion entirely by causing the particles to stick together.

questions.question: If you place a small jelly cube and a large jelly cube into a colored dye, which cube's center will be reached by the dye first?
options: The center of the small cube will be reached first.
The center of both cubes will be reached at the exact same time.
The center of the large cube will be reached first.
Neither cube's center will ever be reached by the dye.

questions.question: How can we explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate at which liquid diffuses into a jelly cube?
options: Higher temperatures make the jelly cube expand to create massive visible gaps.
Particles gain more kinetic energy at higher temperatures, causing them to move and collide faster.
Gravity pulls warmer particles down into the cube much faster.
Warmer liquid particles shrink in size, allowing them to slip through without colliding.

questions.question: What physical property of some substance particles allows them to pass through a selectively-permeable membrane?
options: They are magnetically attracted to the membrane.
They are small enough to pass through the tiny holes in the membrane.
They are square-shaped to match the membrane's pores.
They are extremely heavy and push their way through.

questions.question: When particles diffuse through a selectively-permeable membrane, in which direction do they travel?
options: They only move from the outside to the inside.
They move through the membrane in both directions.
They only move from the inside to the outside.
They move in one direction and then stop moving completely.

questions.question: If there is a higher concentration of a substance outside a selectively-permeable membrane than inside, what is the predicted direction of the net movement of its particles?
options: The net movement of the particles will be from the outside to the inside.
The net movement of the particles will be from the inside to the outside.
There will be absolutely no movement of particles in either direction.
The net movement will randomly change direction every second.

questions.question: When starch and amylase are placed inside Visking tubing, glucose is produced. What observation demonstrates the net movement of a substance through the membrane?
options: The Visking tubing dissolves completely in the water.
Starch is detected in the water outside the tubing.
Glucose is detected in the water outside the tubing.
The water outside the tubing turns completely solid.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the structure of cell cytoplasm and the substances within it?
options: They are made of continuous, non-divisible solid matter.
They are made up of tiny, individual particles.
They consist entirely of empty vacuum with no matter.
They only contain particles when the cell is dead.

questions.question: How do small substance particles, such as oxygen and carbon dioxide, move into and out of a cell?
options: By passing through large tears in the cell wall.
By moving through small holes in the cell membrane.
By being actively pumped through specialized protein gates only.
They cannot pass through because the cell membrane is solid and sealed.

questions.question: Why are some substances, like starch, unable to diffuse through the cell membrane?
options: Their particles are too large to fit through the holes in the cell membrane.
They carry a positive charge which repels the membrane.
Their particles are too small and get trapped inside the membrane pores.
They are made of liquid, and only gases can diffuse.

questions.question: Why is the cell membrane described as 'selectively-permeable'?
options: It allows all substances to pass through without any restriction.
It only allows certain substances to diffuse through it while blocking others.
It prevents all substances from entering or leaving the cell.
It changes its shape to let food in but never lets waste out.

questions.question: What is the direction of the net movement of particles during diffusion through a cell membrane?
options: Up a concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.
Down a concentration gradient, from high to low concentration.
In a circular path around the outside of the membrane.
Always into the cell, regardless of the concentrations.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the movement of particles that undergo diffusion?
options: They move in highly organized parallel lines.
They move in random directions and collide with each other constantly.
They stay completely still until pushed by cell energy.
They only move in clockwise circles.

questions.question: In chemistry and biology, what is meant by the term 'concentration'?
options: The speed at which particles move through a liquid.
The total volume of the container holding a gas.
The number of particles of a substance in a given volume of liquid or gas.
The temperature of a solution.

questions.question: What is the scientific definition of diffusion?
options: The active transport of particles requiring energy from the cell.
The passive movement of particles of a substance from an area of higher to lower concentration.
The movement of water molecules from a concentrated solution to a dilute solution.
The chemical breakdown of large molecules into smaller ones.
